extracted.intended_audience: writers and readers interested in imaginative literature, folklore, and moral/philosophical criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Extractable principles for imaginative writing and moral criticism grounded in Chesterton's Orthodoxy: emphasizes the role of tradition, limits, fairy-tale logic, the healthy use of will, and the preservation of wonder. Useful for authors aiming to balance reason, imagination, and moral standards in storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'wild reason' divorced from life
rubrics_metrics.description: Our mental ruin has been wrought by wild reason, not by wild imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton warns that excessive abstract reasoning, when detached from concrete human facts, leads to intellectual paralysis and moral emptiness (examples: the trajectory of certain modern philosophies leading to 'the emptiness of the asylum'). In practice: avoid making characters, themes, or arguments that are merely schematic abstractions with no rooted human consequences; favor concrete particulars over remote abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject generic praise of 'will' (will-worship is self-defeating)
rubrics_metrics.description: The worship of will is the negation of will. To admire mere choice is to refuse to choose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton argues that praising 'will' in the abstract cannot discriminate between better and worse actions; true volition is always particular. For writers: don't present 'force of will' as a general virtue divorced from concrete ends — instead dramatize particular choices and their limits so the will is meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will entails self-limitation; create via constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Every act of will is an act of self-limitation... To desire action is to desire limitation. The artist loves his limitations: they constitute the THING he is doing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constraint is positive: artistic choices (form, medium, rules) define the work. Chesterton gives concrete images (canvas is flat; sculptor glad clay is colourless; drawing a giraffe requires a long neck) to show limits make art intelligible. In practice: embrace formal and thematic constraints as generative rather than restrictive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art and craft require laws/standards to aim at
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is limitation; the essence of every picture is the frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notion that creativity equals limitless freedom is false; technique, rules, and standards make quality possible. For creative practice: establish clear standards (aesthetic, moral, formal) so satire, praise, or criticism has something to target or uphold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective revolt/critique requires a positive alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: The Jacobin could tell you not only the system he would rebel against, but (what was more important) the system he would NOT rebel against... the new rebel is a Sceptic, and will not entirely trust anything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely opposing an existing state of affairs without proposing or trusting any alternative results in ineffectual criticism. For writers and polemicists: when depicting dissent or crafting satire, supply a coherent standard or constructive vision rather than blanket negation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire presupposes an admitted standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire... presupposes an admitted superiority in certain things over others; it presupposes a standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton notes the decline of strong satire where no common standard exists. Effective satirical writing needs an implicit or explicit value system (e.g., classical standards of beauty, civic virtues) to expose deviation. Anti-pattern: mocking everything without anchoring reference points flattens satire into mere bile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value tradition as collective wisdom (tradition = democracy extended through time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tradition may be defined as an extension of the franchise... Tradition means giving votes to the most obscure of all classes, our ancestors. It is the democracy of the dead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton defends trusting folk wisdom, legends, and common-unity narratives over the isolated claims of specialists. For writers: draw on communal myths, legends, and vernacular forms as authoritative resources rather than treating them as merely primitive or inferior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize the ordinary/common in human portrayal (democratic principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The things common to all men are more important than the things peculiar to any men... democracy classes government among them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton's democratic aesthetic argues that literature should respect ordinary human functions and communal life. For storytelling: focus on shared human experiences (everyday acts, common feelings) rather than only exceptional feats; let ordinary life carry moral weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain childlike wonder and gratitude in tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The strongest emotion was that life was as precious as it was puzzling... The test of all happiness is gratitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A vital component of imaginative writing is preserving a sense of wonder and thankful appreciation for life's mystery. Use language, scenes, and perspective that elicit astonishment and gratitude rather than cynical detachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fairy-tale logic: distinguish logical necessity from observed regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a distinction between a true law (mathematical/logical) and the mere fact of apples falling... When we are asked why eggs turn to birds or fruits fall in autumn, we must answer... MAGIC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton distinguishes laws of reason (necessary relations) from physical facts (regularities we bet on). In imaginative fiction, it's legitimate to invoke 'magic' or enchantment to mark the gap between understanding and occurrence; don't disguise narrative wonder with misleading claims of scientific inevitability. Anti-pattern: treating contingent events as if they were philosophically necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'charm', 'spell', 'enchantment' language over pseudo-scientific 'law' when describing marvels
rubrics_metrics.description: The only words that ever satisfied me as describing Nature are the terms used in the fairy books, 'charm,' 'spell,' 'enchantment.' They express the arbitrariness of the fact and its mystery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing the uncanny or miraculous, use the vocabulary of myth and fairy-tale to preserve mystery; avoid subordinating wonder to mechanistic explanation which flattens it. This stylistic choice keeps magical elements vibrant and philosophically honest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ fairy-tale moral 'statutes' as narrative motifs
rubrics_metrics.description: There is the chivalrous lesson of 'Jack the Giant Killer'... the lesson of 'Cinderella'... 'Beauty and the Beast'... the allegory of the 'Sleeping Beauty'...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton lists concrete moral/ethical lessons embedded in fairy tales (e.g., oppose pride; exalt the humble; love before lovable; death softened). Writers can deploy these archetypal motifs as durable moral templates or thematic signposts, adapting them to new settings while retaining their instructive force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of conflating scientific association with philosophical necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary scientific man is strictly a sentimentalist... he is soaked and swept away by mere associations... he feels as if there must be some dreamy, tender connection between the two ideas, whereas there is none.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton criticizes treating frequent conjunctions as showing inner necessity (e.g., moon→tide). For writers: be cautious using scientific metaphor as a narrative crutch that implies deeper meaning; distinguish evocative metaphor from false causal claims. Use association deliberately, but do not mistake it for proof or philosophic law.
